title: Testing Services: Pyramid to Production
summary: Quick revision notes on testing backend services: the test pyramid, unit and component tests, Pact consumer-driven contracts, Testcontainers integration tests, end-to-end test costs, and testing in production.

chapters.title: Service Test Pyramid Mental Model
points: Test pyramid: many fast unit tests at the base, fewer component/integration tests in the middle, very few end-to-end tests at the top
Each layer up trades speed and determinism for realism: slower, flakier, costlier to debug, but closer to production
Microservices add a contract layer between services; the pyramid is often reshaped as a 'honeycomb' that is heavy on integration tests when services have little internal logic
Rule of thumb: push every check to the lowest layer that can catch the bug; a failing E2E test should be a signal to add a lower-level test
Ice-cream cone anti-pattern: mostly manual and E2E tests with few unit tests gives slow feedback and flaky suites

chapters.title: Unit and Component Tests
points: Unit test: one class or function in isolation, no network or disk, runs in milliseconds; solitary tests mock collaborators, sociable tests use real ones
Component test: one whole service tested through its public API (HTTP or messages) with its external dependencies replaced by in-process fakes or stubs
Test doubles: stub returns canned answers, mock verifies interactions, fake is a working lightweight implementation (in-memory repository)
Example: start the app in-process (e.g. Spring MockMvc or FastAPI TestClient), stub the downstream HTTP client with WireMock, assert on the response and status code
Mistake: over-mocking so tests assert implementation details and break on every refactor; test behaviour and outputs instead

chapters.title: Consumer-Driven Contract Tests with Pact
points: Contract test: verifies that a consumer's expectations of a provider's API and the provider's real behaviour agree, without deploying both together
Consumer side: write a test against a Pact mock provider; it records the request and expected response into a pact JSON file
Provider side: Pact replays the recorded requests against the real provider and verifies the responses match; provider states (given 'user 1 exists') set up the data
Pact Broker (or PactFlow) stores pacts and verification results; can-i-deploy checks whether a version is safe to release against its integration partners
Mistakes: asserting every field instead of only what the consumer uses, using exact values instead of matchers (like(), eachLike(), regex), treating Pact as functional testing of the provider

chapters.title: Integration Tests with Testcontainers
points: Testcontainers: a library that starts real throwaway Docker containers (Postgres, Kafka, Redis, LocalStack) from test code and removes them afterwards via the Ryuk reaper
Integration tests exercise your code against a real dependency, catching SQL dialect, migration, serialization and driver bugs that in-memory fakes like H2 miss
Example (Java): @Container static PostgreSQLContainer<?> pg = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16"); then wire pg.getJdbcUrl() into the datasource via @DynamicPropertySource
Speed tips: use a static or singleton container shared across test classes, reuse mode locally, pin image tags, and reset data between tests with truncate or transactions
Mistakes: using latest image tags, hard-coded ports instead of the mapped port from getMappedPort(), and waiting with sleeps instead of a wait strategy

chapters.title: End-to-End Tests and Testing in Production
points: E2E test: drives the fully deployed system through its real entry point (UI or public API) across all services and datastores
Costs: slow, flaky from timing and shared environments, hard to debug which service failed, and a shared staging environment becomes a bottleneck
Keep E2E to a handful of critical user journeys (login, checkout) and run them as smoke tests after deploy, not for every edge case
Testing in production: feature flags, canary releases, blue-green deploys, synthetic monitoring probes, and dark launches or traffic shadowing validate real behaviour with limited blast radius
Mistakes: testing in production without observability and fast rollback, and writing test data into real customer records without isolation or cleanup

chapters.title: Service Testing Cheat Sheet
points: Layers: unit (ms, isolated) > component (one service, stubbed deps) > contract (Pact) > integration (Testcontainers) > E2E (few journeys)
Pact flow: consumer test writes pact, publish to Broker, provider verifies, can-i-deploy gates release
Testcontainers: real dependency in Docker, pin tags, use mapped ports and wait strategies, share containers across classes
Place each check at the lowest layer that can catch the bug; E2E only for critical journeys
Production safety net: feature flags, canary, synthetic probes, plus metrics, alerts and fast rollback
